name: Bright Blue
lede: Bright Blue is the xkcd survey's name for a saturated blue, and a phrase the color books use for lapis, azure and cornflower alike.

sections.title: A name from a survey
sections.body:
Bright Blue, as a color on our list, comes from a survey rather than a tradition [1]. The xkcd color survey, published on 3 May 2010, gathered over five million color names from 222,500 sessions, and it set each name's color at the spot in RGB space where the most people chose that name [1]. Our library records Bright Blue from that survey, filed as a plain modifier plus a basic color word [2]. The phrase itself is plain, undated and nobody's coinage.

The survey's swatch, #0165FC, is a saturated blue leaning slightly toward violet [2]. It is a vivid blue in the ISCC-NBS system of 1955, 7 CIEDE2000 units from that class's center [2]. Our curriculum Blue (#2563C9) is 6 units away, the pure screen blue `blue` (#0000FF) is 19 away, and the survey's own plain "blue" (#0343DF) is 11 away [2]. Bright Blue is therefore a punchier blue than the one we teach first, but not the electric extreme of the screen primary [2]. Beside it on the shelf sit [[lapis-lazuli]], [[blue]], [[royal-blue]] and [[electric-blue]] [2].

sections.title: What the books mean by it
sections.body:
The books never pin the phrase to one color [3][4][5]. They use the phrase the way a person describes a color to someone who cannot see it. Paterson's dictionary glosses *azure* as bright blue, often the blue of a cloudless sky, and [[gem:lapis-lazuli|lapis lazuli]] as a bright blue, a mineral he says was used to make ultramarine from the 13th century [3]. St Clair's glossary defines cornflower as a bright blue with a little violet and cyan as a bright blue with a little green [4]. The Pigment Compendium calls the mineral azurite a bright blue hydrated copper carbonate [5].

In each case "bright blue" is the plain starting point and the modifier says which way it leans. That is useful for the reader, because it means our swatch sits near the middle of what the phrase has covered: a clean, strong blue with a slight pull to violet, between a green-leaning cyan and a violet-leaning cornflower [4][2].

sections.title: A blue that meant rank
sections.body:
Whether a bright blue was admired depends on the century. Pastoureau reports that in Rome bright blue was considered ugly, and that blue clothing marked eccentricity or mourning [6]. A stable bright blue dye became possible in the thirteenth century, ending what he calls the somber, grey and washed-out blues of earlier centuries, and the color moved from the work clothes of artisans to aristocratic dress [7].

Greenfield writes that by the 1400s the lapis-like bright blue counted as a noble color, while pale blue stayed with servants and laborers [8]. Rank was written into law: Pastoureau notes that in Italy some patricians and merchants were forbidden certain bright blues, such as the Florentine peacock blues, and turned to black as a result [9]. St Clair adds that from the twelfth century the Virgin was increasingly shown in bright blue robes, having earlier worn dark colors of mourning, and that the pigment most associated with her was ultramarine [10].

Bright blue also reached the wardrobe. Greenfield says Henry VIII owned bright blue and red doublets, and that in the 1860s the new synthetic dyes put crinolines in emerald green, bright blue and magenta [11][12].

sections.title: Painters and their bright blues
sections.body:
Painters have treated bright blue as a risk. Caravaggio's early biographer Bellori said the painter had no interest in beautiful single colors such as vermilion and bright blues, which he kept subdued [13]. Ball dates a reversal to 1897, when Matisse dropped a sombre palette for one of bright blues, greens and reds from newly invented pigments, as the Impressionists had done [14].

Brands used the same idea. Pastoureau notes that the bright blue of the Gauloises cigarette packs, introduced in 1910, became an emblem of France, and the name even became a colloquial term for a light greyish blue with a touch of violet [15]. Outside art, St Clair observes that sparks and St Elmo's fire, the glow on ships' masts, are bright blue, sometimes tinted with violet, and that pale bright blue has become the popular color of electricity [16].

Gage quotes a passage from *The Hall* about a peacock whose feathers are bright blue in the sun and bright green in shadow, a reminder that a bright blue can come from structure and light rather than from a dye [17].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Bright Blue is almost absent from the museum record we have [18]. By the strictest lens, no painting in our archive of 23,781 has this color covering one per cent of the canvas within a CIEDE2000 distance of 4 [18]. With a looser match, within 10 units and at least two per cent of the canvas, 18 works qualify [18]. That is 0.08 per cent of the archive [18].

The leaders are Albert Marquet's [[painting:commons-Q21730955|View of Saint-Jean-de-Luz]] of 1907, with a blue patch of 24 per cent, and Alphonse Osbert's [[painting:commons-Q17494748|Paysage avec le Sphinx]] of 1900 at 19 per cent [18]. The list also includes Wouwerman's [[painting:nga-218605|The Departure for the Hunt]] of 1665 and Michelangelo's [[painting:commons-Q1473546|Doni Tondo]] of about 1500, both near 18 per cent [18]. The earliest in the archive is Fra Angelico's [[painting:commons-Q22082602|Madonna of the Pomegranate]] of 1426, at 13 per cent [18]. These are photographs of paintings, often of cloaks and skies, and sometimes of varnish that has altered the blue [18].

The honest reading is that this bright blue is a modern screen color, and the paintings with it are mostly blue skies and robes whose color has survived. The plain word *blue* is far more common in printed English than any of these details suggest, but that is a fact about the word, not this swatch [18].

choices: A plain strong starting point, with other words saying which way it leans
questions.answer: A plain strong starting point, with other words saying which way it leans

questions.q: In fifteenth-century Europe bright blue, the shade of lapis lazuli, was seen as a noble color.

openers: Our Bright Blue comes from a 2010 online survey of 222,500 sessions.
In Rome, writes Pastoureau, bright blue was considered ugly; by the 1400s it was noble.

issues: Fixed chronology: Virgin in bright blue is twelfth century (St Clair), not 'the same time' as the 1400s.
Reworded 'meaning flipped again with chemistry' (Henry VIII doublets are Renaissance; claim was overstated).
Attributed the lapis/ultramarine 13th-century date to Paterson.
xkcd survey facts rest on the survey's own post, not a book.
